Gene Sarazen, born Eugenio Saraceni. An Italian-American professional golfer who won 7 major championships and established himself as one of golf's foundational figures of the early twentieth century. Known for inventing the sand wedge and for his longevity competing across five decades, he was instrumental in professionalizing the sport.

He won 7 major championships: 3 US Opens in 1922, 1932, and 1935, 2 PGA Championships in 1922 and 1923, 1 Masters in 1935, and 1 Open Championship in 1932. He invented the sand wedge in the 1930s, revolutionizing short-game technique and forever altering how golf is played. One of golf's most famous shots is his double eagle, also called an albatross, at the 15th hole during the 1935 Masters, which helped him win that tournament.

Sarazen competed professionally from 1921 until well into the 1970s, demonstrating extraordinary competitive longevity across five decades. He won 39 PGA Tour events and numerous international tournaments, establishing himself as a global competitor. He pioneered teaching and instruction, mentoring younger players and establishing the pedagogy of professional golf. He remained a visible and respected figure in golf throughout his life, attending tournaments and mentoring into his 90s.
